definition: Semi-global matching (SGM) is a computer vision algorithm for the estimation of a dense disparity map from a rectified stereo image pair, introduced in 2005 by Heiko Hirschmüller while working at the German Aerospace Center.
details: Given its predictable run time, its favourable trade-off between quality of the results and computing time, and its suitability for fast parallel implementation in ASIC or FPGA, it has encountered wide adoption in real-time stereo vision applications such as robotics and advanced driver assistance systems.

explainer.lead: Semi-global matching estimates a dense disparity map from a rectified stereo image pair, introduced by Heiko Hirschmüller in 2005 at the German Aerospace Center. Its predictable runtime and quality-to-time trade-off made it a workhorse for real-time stereo.

tiers.eli5: Two cameras look at the same scene, and the algorithm works out how far each pixel shifted between the two views to judge depth.
tiers.practitioner: It is widely used in robotics and driver assistance because it parallelises well in ASIC or FPGA hardware. A pitfall is that it depends on rectified stereo pairs, so calibration and rectification must be right first.
tiers.paperLevel: A computer vision algorithm for dense disparity estimation from a rectified stereo image pair, with predictable runtime and a favourable trade-off between result quality and computing time.

explainer.example: A car's stereo camera pair feeds rectified images to SGM, which outputs a depth map for obstacle detection.
